According to these theories, the fundamental laws of physics are invariant and apply uniformly to all inertial reference frames (frames of motion where an observer is not accelerating), regardless of their state of motion.

One of the key predictions of the theory of relativity is that time does not have a preferred direction; rather, time progresses uniformly for all observers in an inertial frame. However, time can appear to move slower for objects moving at relativistic speeds relative to another observer, or for observers near very massive objects in strong gravitational fields, according to the effects of special relativity and general relativity, respectively.

In everyday observations, we do not notice this difference because our velocities and masses are so small that the corrections predicted by the theory are extremely tiny, even if they exist. For example, observing atomic clocks on airplanes vs. those on the ground shows that the clocks in the airplane tick slightly slower due to the faster rate of acceleration and deceleration of the aircraft.

So, while strictly speaking time always flows forward in the same direction as observed from any inertial frame, there are situations where the effects of relativity mean that time appears to be "flowing" more slowly or appearing to progress differently when viewed from different frames or under different conditions. But fundamentally, time moves forward in the same direction as measured in all inertial frames. 

To summarize, time flows forward uniformly for all observers in an inertial frame, but it does not change direction under any circumstances. The perceived difference between frames moving relatively to each other is more a question of synchronization and the effects of special relativity on relative measurements than a fundamental change in the direction of time itself.
